definition: Ascetic means practicing strict self-denial as a form of discipline.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ascetic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ascetic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The philosophy professor lived an ascetic life by choice: one rented room, two sets of clothes, and plain rice dinners, though her salary could buy far more.
A sparing diner skips dessert now and then; ascetic describes someone who has sworn off dessert - and most other comforts - as a standing rule.
A spartan room is bare and comfortless, but the word describes the surroundings; ascetic goes further, naming a person's deliberate discipline of self-denial behind that bareness.

Abstinent means refraining from one particular pleasure - alcohol, sweets, screens - often for health or a vow. Ascetic sweeps far wider: an ascetic person gives up comfort across the board, as a standing discipline of self-denial, not one renounced indulgence.

Self-denying people give things up, often so that others can have more - the parent who skips lunch so the children eat. Ascetic self-denial points inward: comforts surrendered as a deliberate discipline to sharpen the mind or spirit, not as a sacrifice made for someone else.

Austere describes severity and plainness - an austere office, a plain gray suit, a stern manner - and it judges how something looks or feels. Ascetic names the practice behind such bareness: a person deliberately denying themselves comfort as a discipline of mind or spirit.

Ascetic comes from Greek askein, 'to exercise or train.' The ancient Greeks used asketes for athletes in hard training; English borrowed only the spiritual sense, and no other common English word ever grew from the root.
Ascetic means practicing strict self-denial as a form of discipline.
The chess grandmaster spent the six weeks before the title match in an ascetic routine: plain meals, dawn walks, no phone, no visitors.
Comfort, he told his team, dulls calculation, and he wanted his mind stripped as bare as his training table.

Ascetic is stronger than 'simple' or 'strict' because it names self-denial chosen as a discipline - giving up comfort on purpose to sharpen the mind or spirit, not merely doing without because money is short.
Ascetic marks the extreme end of self-denial: comfort given up on purpose, as a discipline.
Keep it apart from spartan, which describes bare conditions rather than a person's chosen practice - a cheap motel room is spartan, a hermit's chosen bare hut is ascetic.
